claim: African trypanosomes are the causative agents of neglected tropical diseases affecting both humans and livestock.
source: African trypanosomes are the causative agents of neglected tropical diseases affecting both humans and livestock.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about African trypanosomes and their role in causing neglected tropical diseases.

claim: Disease control of African trypanosomiasis is highly challenging due to an increasing number of drug treatment failures.
source: Disease control is highly challenging due to an increasing number of drug treatment failures.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to the literature on drug treatment failures in the context of the manuscript.

claim: African trypanosomes are extracellular, blood-borne parasites that mainly rely on glycolysis for their energy metabolism within the mammalian host.
source: African trypanosomes are extracellular, blood-borne parasites that mainly rely on glycolysis for their energy metabolism within the mammalian host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the metabolic characteristics of African trypanosomes in their mammalian hosts.

claim: Trypanosomal glycolytic enzymes are of interest for the development of trypanocidal drugs.
source: Trypanosomal glycolytic enzymes are therefore of interest for the development of trypanocidal drugs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic dependence of trypanosomes on glycolysis and established drug development strategies.

claim: A camelid single-domain antibody (sdAb42) selectively inhibits the enzymatic activity of trypanosomatid pyruvate kinases through an allosteric mechanism.
source: Here, we report the serendipitous discovery of a camelid single-domain antibody (sdAb aka Nanobody) that selectively inhibits the enzymatic activity of trypanosomatid (but not host) pyruvate kinases through an allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from enzyme kinetics, biophysics, and structural biology presented in the manuscript.

claim: sdAb-mediated enzyme inhibition negatively impacts parasite fitness and growth.
source: By combining enzyme kinetics, biophysics, structural biology, and transgenic parasite survival assays, we provide a proof-of-principle that the sdAb-mediated enzyme inhibition negatively impacts parasite fitness and growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by transgenic parasite survival assays and growth curve analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neglected tropical diseases affect more than 1 billion people worldwide.
source: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) comprise a wide variety of communicable diseases that are prevalent in (sub)tropical regions and affect more than 1 billion people worldwide.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from the literature.

claim: NTDs constitute a major health threat in both developing and developed countries, with those living in poverty being especially vulnerable.
source: It is becoming increasingly clear that NTDs constitute a major health threat in both developing and developed countries, with those living in poverty being especially vulnerable (Hunter, 2014; Picado et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hunter, 2014 and Picado et al., 2019.

claim: NTDs are typically characterized by a low mortality and high morbidity.
source: NTDs are typically characterized by a low mortality and high morbidity, which results in a severe impact on the quality of life and economic productivity of those affected.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the characteristics of neglected tropical diseases.

claim: NTD control has become more complicated by globalization, human migration, climate change and the altered distribution of disease-transmitting vectors.
source: In recent times, NTD control has become more complicated by globalization, human migration, climate change and the altered distribution of disease-transmitting vectors (including mosquitoes, flies, and ticks).
evidence: This is an inference based on current trends and their impact on disease control.

claim: The WHO has listed 20 NTDs that should be tackled in the interest of global health and well-being.
source: The WHO has listed 20 NTDs that should be tackled in the interest of global health and well-being (https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/diseases/en).
evidence: This is a factual statement about WHO's classification, supported by a reference to the WHO website.

claim: Three of the WHO-listed NTDs are caused by trypanosomatids.
source: Three of these are caused by trypanosomatids, a group of flagellated, single-celled eukaryotic organisms comprising parasites of the Trypanosoma and Leishmania genera.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the causative agents of certain NTDs.

claim: The development of an effective vaccine against trypanosomes is thwarted by sophisticated immune-evasion strategies.
source: However, the development of an effective vaccine against these parasites is thwarted by sophisticated immune-evasion strategies (Pays et al., 2023), while vector control may be hampered due to resistance of the insect vector to insecticides (Field et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pays et al., 2023 and Field et al., 2017.

claim: Vector control may be hampered due to resistance of the insect vector to insecticides.
source: However, the development of an effective vaccine against these parasites is thwarted by sophisticated immune-evasion strategies (Pays et al., 2023), while vector control may be hampered due to resistance of the insect vector to insecticides (Field et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Field et al., 2017.

claim: Chemotherapy is an essential pillar for clinical management, control and/or elimination of trypanosomiasis.
source: As a result, chemotherapy is an essential pillar for clinical management, control and/or elimination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of vaccination and vector control strategies.

claim: A number of reports describe treatment failure or parasite resistance to the currently available drugs for trypanosomiasis.
source: Unfortunately, a number of reports describe treatment failure or parasite resistance to the currently available drugs (De Rycker et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to De Rycker et al., 2018.

claim: There is a need for alternative compounds for trypanosomiasis treatment, preferably with novel modes of action.
source: Hence, there is a need for alternative compounds, preferably with novel modes of action and/or designed based on mechanistic insights of the target's structure-function relationship (Field et al., 2017; De Rycker et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the problem of drug resistance, supported by citations to Field et al., 2017 and De Rycker et al., 2018.

claim: AAT strongly impedes sustainable livestock rearing in Sub-Saharan Africa.
source: This need is especially pressing for AAT, which strongly impedes sustainable livestock rearing in Sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the impact of AAT on livestock in Sub-Saharan Africa.

claim: AAT results in drastic reductions of draft power, meat, and milk production by infected animals.
source: AAT results in drastic reductions of draft power, meat, and milk production by the infected animals (small and large ruminants), and its control relies mainly on vector control and chemotherapy, with only few drugs currently available.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the effects of AAT on livestock productivity.

claim: The lack of routine field diagnosis has resulted in the misuse of trypanocidal drugs, thereby accelerating the rise of parasite resistance.
source: The lack of routine field diagnosis has resulted in the misuse of trypanocidal drugs, thereby accelerating the rise of parasite resistance and further exacerbating the problem (Richards et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Richards et al., 2021.

claim: AAT-inflicted annual losses are estimated at around $5 billion.
source: As such, AAT-inflicted annual losses are estimated at around $ 5 billion (and the necessity to invest another $ 30 million each year to control AAT through chemotherapy), thereby having a devastating impact on the socio-economic development of Sub-Saharan Africa (Fetene et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fetene et al., 2021.

claim: HAT has reached a post-elimination phase as a public health problem with less than 1000 yearly documented cases.
source: In contrast, HAT is perceived as a minor threat as it has reached a post-elimination phase as a public health problem with less than 1000 yearly documented cases (Franco et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Franco et al., 2022.

claim: New and effective drugs for HAT treatment have recently become available.
source: In addition, new and effective drugs for HAT treatment have recently become available (De Rycker et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to De Rycker et al., 2023.

claim: HAT control currently relies on case detection and treatment, and vector control.
source: HAT control currently relies on case detection and treatment, and vector control (Büscher et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Büscher et al., 2017.

claim: African trypanosomes have a bipartite life cycle involving insect vectors and mammals as hosts.
source: African trypanosomes are extracellular parasites that have a bipartite life cycle involving insect vectors and mammals as hosts (Radwanska et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Radwanska et al., 2018.

claim: Most HAT and AAT causing trypanosomes are uniquely vectored by tsetse flies and are confined to Sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Most HAT (T. brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense) and AAT (T. b. brucei and T. congolense) causing trypanosomes are uniquely vectored by tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) and are confined to Sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the geographic distribution and vectors of African trypanosomes.

claim: T. b. evansi and T. vivax have expanded beyond the tsetse belt due to their ability to be mechanically transmitted by a variety of biting flies.
source: T. b. evansi and T. vivax (both causative agents of AAT) have expanded beyond the tsetse belt due to their ability to be mechanically transmitted by a variety of biting flies (Glossina, Stomoxys, and Tabanus spp.).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transmission mechanisms of certain trypanosome species.

claim: T. b. equiperdum infects equids and is transmitted directly from animal to animal through sexual contact.
source: Finally, T. b. equiperdum infects equids and represents an exception as it is transmitted directly from animal to animal through sexual contact.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transmission mechanism of T. b. equiperdum.

claim: The predominant parasite form within the mammalian host is called the bloodstream form (BSF).
source: For all African trypanosomes, the predominant parasite form within the mammalian host is called the bloodstream form (BSF) which, as the name suggests, resides mainly inside the host bloodstream.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the life cycle stages of African trypanosomes.

claim: The BSF colonizes sites such as the lymphatics, the skin, brain, testes, adipose tissue, and lungs.
source: The BSF also colonizes sites such as the lymphatics, the skin, brain, testes, adipose tissue, and lungs (Trindade et al., 2016; Caljon et al., 2016; Capewell et al., 2016; Krüger et al., 2018; Mabille et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Trindade et al., 2016; Caljon et al., 2016; Capewell et al., 2016; Krüger et al., 2018; Mabille et al., 2022).

claim: The BSF has steady access to high blood glucose concentrations (∼5 mM) and has evolved to exclusively rely on glycolysis to power its metabolism.
source: Given its niche, the BSF has steady access to high blood glucose concentrations (∼5 mM) and has evolved to exclusively rely on glycolysis to power its metabolism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the metabolic characteristics of the bloodstream form of trypanosomes.

claim: Most trypanosomal glycolytic enzymes are localized in organelles called glycosomes.
source: For this reason, trypanosomal glycolytic enzymes (of which most are localized in organelles called glycosomes Szöör et al., 2014; Haanstra et al., 2016; Figure 1A) have received much interest and attention as targets for the development of trypanocidal compounds (Bakker et al., 2000; Verlinde et al., 2001; Haanstra and Bakker, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szöör et al., 2014 and Haanstra et al., 2016, and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: RNAi experiments have shown that a reduction in glycolytic flux induces growth impairment and eventually leads to parasite death.
source: Indeed, informed by computational models of trypanosomal glycolysis, RNAi experiments have shown that a reduction in glycolytic flux induces growth impairment and eventually leads to parasite death (Albert et al., 2005; Haanstra et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Albert et al., 2005 and Haanstra et al., 2011.

claim: A novel and selective small-molecule inhibitor of the trypanosomal glycolytic enzyme phosphofructokinase (PFK) was developed that impairs PFK activity via an allosteric mechanism and leads to parasite death in vitro and in vivo.
source: This principle was recently successfully exploited by McNae, Kinkead, Malik and co-workers, who developed a novel and selective small-molecule inhibitor of the trypanosomal glycolytic enzyme phosphofructokinase (PFK; McNae et al., 2021). The compound impairs PFK activity via an allosteric mechanism and was validated to lead to parasite death in vitro as well as in an in vivo mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McNae et al., 2021.

claim: Pyruvate kinase (PYK) catalyses the last step of glycolysis, the irreversible conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate.
source: Pyruvate kinase (PYK) represents another attractive glycolytic target. This non-glycosomal enzyme catalyses the last step of the glycolysis (the irreversible conversion of phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic function of pyruvate kinase, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The PYK reaction generates ATP through the transfer of a phosphoryl group from PEP to ADP.
source: The importance of this reaction is twofold: (i) the generation of ATP through the transfer of a phosphoryl group from PEP to ADP and (ii) the formation of pyruvate, a crucial metabolite of the central metabolism.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the biochemical function of pyruvate kinase.

claim: Trypanosomatid PYKs are homotetramers.
source: Like most PYKs, trypanosomatid PYKs are homotetramers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the quaternary structure of trypanosomatid pyruvate kinases.

claim: The PYK monomer is a ∼55 kDa protein organized into four domains termed 'N', 'A', 'B', and 'C'.
source: The PYK monomer is a ∼55 kDa protein organized into four domains termed 'N', 'A', 'B', and 'C' (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of PYK, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The B domain is known as the flexible 'lid' domain that shields the active site during enzyme-mediated phosphotransfer.
source: The B domain is known as the flexible 'lid' domain that shields the active site during enzyme-mediated phosphotransfer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the PYK B domain.

claim: The C domain harbors the binding pocket for allosteric effectors and stabilizes the PYK tetramer by formation of CC' dimer interfaces.
source: Finally, the C domain harbors the binding pocket for allosteric effectors and stabilizes the PYK tetramer by formation of CC' dimer interfaces.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of the PYK C domain.

claim: The activity of trypanosomatid PYKs is tightly regulated through an allosteric mechanism known as the 'rock and lock' model.
source: Because of their role in ATP production and distribution of fluxes into different metabolic branches, the activity of trypanosomatid PYKs is tightly regulated through an allosteric mechanism known as the 'rock and lock' model (Morgan et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2014; Pinto Torres et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morgan et al., 2010; Morgan et al., 2014; and Pinto Torres et al., 2020.

claim: The binding of substrates and/or effectors to the active and effector sites triggers a conformational change from the enzymatically inactive T state to the catalytically active R state.
source: In this model (which is detailed in Figure 1C), the binding of substrates and/or effectors (and analogs thereof) to the active and effector sites, respectively, trigger a conformational change from the enzymatically inactive T state to the catalytically active R state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the 'rock and lock' mechanism, illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Known effector molecules for trypanosomatid PYKs are fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F26BP), fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (F16BP) and sulfate (SO42-), with F26BP being the most potent one.
source: Known effector molecules for trypanosomatid PYKs are fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F26BP), fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (F16BP) and sulfate (SO42-), with F26BP being the most potent one (van Schaftingen et al., 1985; Callens and Opperdoes, 1992; Ernest et al., 1994; Tulloch et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to van Schaftingen et al., 1985; Callens and Opperdoes, 1992; Ernest et al., 1994; and Tulloch et al., 2008.

claim: Trypanosomatid PYKs seem to be largely unresponsive to the allosteric regulation of enzyme activity by free amino acids.
source: Interestingly, trypanosomatid PYKs seem to be largely unresponsive to the allosteric regulation of enzyme activity by free amino acids (Callens et al., 1991), which contrasts with human PYKs (Chaneton et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Callens et al., 1991; Chaneton et al., 2012; and Yuan et al., 2018.

claim: Known trypanosomatid PYK inhibitors impair enzymatic activity through occupation of the PYK active site.
source: Known trypanosomatid PYK inhibitors impair enzymatic activity through occupation of the PYK active site (Morgan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morgan et al., 2011.

claim: sdAb42 is a potent inhibitor of TcoPYK with an IC50 value of around 15 nM.
source: While complexation of TcoPYK with sdAb44 and a negative control sdAb (BCII10) have no impact, the addition of increasing sdAb42 concentrations severely reduces (and even completely abolishes) enzymatic activity with an IC50 value of around 15 nM (Figure 2, panels A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, panels A and B.

claim: The inhibition displayed by sdAb42 is selective for TcoPYK as no effect on the enzymatic activity of human PYK could be observed.
source: Moreover, the inhibition displayed by sdAb42 is selective for TcoPYK as no effect on the enzymatic activity of human PYK could be observed (even at a 1000-fold sdAb excess, Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Four sdAb42 molecules are bound to the TcoPYK tetramer.
source: A general overview of the crystal structure reveals that four sdAb42 molecules are bound to the TcoPYK tetramer (Figure 3A), which is in accordance with the stoichiometry in solution, previously determined via analytical gel filtration (Pinto Torres et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3A and previous analytical gel filtration data cited from Pinto Torres et al., 2018.

claim: The epitope of a single sdAb42 spans a region across two TcoPYK subunits linked together along the AA' dimer interface.
source: Interestingly, the epitope of a single sdAb42 spans a region across two TcoPYK subunits linked together along the AA' dimer interface (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: sdAb42-bound TcoPYK resides in its inactive T state.
source: A comparison of the conformation of sdAb42-bound TcoPYK to the enzyme's R state structure and an inspection of the tell-tale features of T and R state trypanosomatid PYK conformations (Figure 1C) show that the enzyme resides in its inactive T state when interacting with sdAb42 (the signature Arg311 flip is displayed in Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data and structural comparisons shown in Figures 1C and 3C.

claim: sdAb42 significantly stabilises apo TcoPYK, leading to an increase in the enzyme's thermal stability (ΔTm,app = 10.3°C).
source: Third, thermal unfolding followed by CD spectroscopy shows that sdAb42 significantly stabilises apo TcoPYK (Figure 3E). In accordance with our previous findings (Pinto Torres et al., 2020), apo TcoPYK displays an apparent melting temperature (Tm,app) of ∼46 °C. The binding of sdAb42 leads to a remarkable increase in the enzyme's thermal stability (ΔTm,app = 10.3°C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectroscopy data shown in Figure 3E and cited from Pinto Torres et al., 2020.

claim: sdAb42 impairs TcoPYK activity by selectively binding and stabilising the enzyme's inactive T state.
source: When taken together, the data strongly indicate that sdAb42 impairs TcoPYK activity by selectively binding and stabilising the enzyme's inactive T state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystallographic, CD spectroscopy, and enzyme kinetics data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The sdAb42 epitope largely coincides with an 'allosteric hotspot' located on the enzyme's surface.
source: The ACI predictions performed on the TcoPYK T and R state tetramer structures reveal that the sdAb42 epitope largely coincides with an 'allosteric hotspot' located on the enzyme's surface (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The TcoPYK residues contacted by sdAb42's CDR1 (Arg20, Ser44, Val348, Ile352) display high ACI values (>0.75).
source: Especially the TcoPYK residues contacted by sdAb42's CDR1 (Arg20, Ser44, Val348, Ile352) display high ACI values (>0.75) implying that a perturbation of these residues will have a high probability of propagating to the active site and, hence, affecting enzyme activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation analysis data.

claim: The ACI values of the sdAb42 epitope residues are higher in the T state compared to the R state tetramer.
source: Interestingly, the ACI values of these residues are higher in the T state compared to the R state tetramer, which implies that the allosteric coupling between the sdAb42-recognized 'allosteric hotspot' and the enzyme's active site appears to be stronger in the T state conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation analysis data comparing T and R state structures.

claim: In the TcoPYK T state tetramer, the allosteric pathways can be defined as 'intersubunit' since they run from the effector site in one subunit to the active site of a second subunit across the AA' interface.
source: In the TcoPYK T state tetramer, the allosteric pathways can be defined as 'intersubunit' since they run from the effector site in one subunit to the active site of a second subunit across the AA' interface.
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the R state, the communication pathways link up the active and effector sites within individual monomers and can be considered as 'intrasubunit'.
source: In contrast, the R state communication pathways link up the active and effector sites within individual monomers and can thus be considered as "intrasubunit".
evidence: This claim is supported by perturbation analysis data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The sdAb42 epitope is well conserved among trypanosomatids.
source: Mapping the degree of sequence conservation onto the structure of TcoPYK clearly illustrates that the sdAb42 epitope is well conserved among trypanosomatids (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: As little as three epitope residues differ between TcoPYK and T. brucei/L. mexicana PYK: Lys43 (Gln43 in LmePYK), Val348 (Ala348 in LmePYK), and Ile352 (Val352 and Leu352 in TbrPYK and LmePYK, respectively).
source: Upon comparison with the sequences and structures of T. brucei and L. mexicana PYK (TbrPYK and LmePYK, respectively; two reference enzymes for studying the structure-function relationship of trypanosomatid PYKs), as little as three epitope residues differ: Lys43 (Gln43 in LmePYK), Val348 (Ala348 in LmePYK), and Ile352 (Val352 and Leu352 in TbrPYK and LmePYK, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment and structural comparison data.

claim: sdAb42 binds TcoPYK with a high affinity in the low nM range (KD = 0.90 ± 0.07 nM).
source: As previously determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR; Pinto Torres et al., 2018), sdAb42 binds TcoPYK with a high affinity in the low nM range (KD = 0.90 ± 0.07 nM), while the affinity of sdAb42 for TbrPYK and LmePYK is roughly 40-fold lower (KD values of 37.16 ± 14.80 nM and 42.54 ± 10.81 nM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B and Table 3, and cited SPR data from Pinto Torres et al., 2018.

claim: The affinity of sdAb42 for TbrPYK and LmePYK is roughly 40-fold lower than for TcoPYK (KD values of 37.16 ± 14.80 nM and 42.54 ± 10.81 nM, respectively).
source: As previously determined by surface plasmon resonance (SPR; Pinto Torres et al., 2018), sdAb42 binds TcoPYK with a high affinity in the low nM range (KD = 0.90 ± 0.07 nM), while the affinity of sdAb42 for TbrPYK and LmePYK is roughly 40-fold lower (KD values of 37.16 ± 14.80 nM and 42.54 ± 10.81 nM, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B and Table 3.

claim: The addition of sdAb42 to TbrPYK and LmePYK impairs enzyme activity in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, the addition of sdAb42 to TbrPYK and LmePYK also impairs enzyme activity in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: sdAb42 displays slow-binding inhibition kinetics against trypanosomatid PYKs.
source: A careful inspection of the collected activity curves reveals the presence of non-linear features in the early phases, which is exacerbated with increasing inhibitor concentrations (especially pronounced for TcoPYK; Figure 6, top inset). Such non-linear behavior is typical for so-called 'slow-binding inhibition', which can indeed be explained by the requirement of a TcoPYK R- to T-state transition prior to sdAb42-mediated enzyme inhibition, thereby supporting the above-mentioned hypothesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: sdAb42 inhibits TcoPYK with an IC50 of ∼350 nM under conditions where the enzyme is first saturated with substrate and effector molecules.
source: In this way we find that sdAb42 inhibits TcoPYK with an IC50 of ∼350 nM, from which two observations can be made.
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme kinetics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The IC50-value determined under conditions where TcoPYK is first saturated with substrate and effector is roughly 24-fold higher compared to the IC50 measured when TcoPYK is first incubated with sdAb42.
source: First, the IC50-value determined under these assay conditions is roughly 24-fold higher compared to the IC50 measured under assay conditions in which TcoPYK is first incubated with sdAb42 prior to the addition of substrate and effector molecules (Figure 2C), which indeed confirms that enzyme inhibition is less efficient under these circumstances.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of IC50 values from different experimental conditions shown in Figures 2C and 6.

claim: The production of sdAb42 as an 'intrabody' induces a growth defect in transgenic T. brucei lines.
source: The data presented in Figure 7A clearly demonstrate that (i) the intrabodies could successfully be produced upon Tet induction and that (ii) sdAb42 appears to induce a growth defect in a dose-dependent manner while BCII10 does not.
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Increasing sdAb42 expression levels lead to larger growth defects in T. brucei.
source: This reveals that increasing sdAb42 expression levels lead to larger growth defects, supporting a positive correlation between intrabody levels and impaired fitness (Pearson correlation, r=0.95; Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve and fluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: BCII10 levels have no impact on parasite growth.
source: As expected, BCII10 levels have no impact on parasite growth (Pearson correlation, r=–0.72), even at median fluorescence intensity (MFI) values that are significantly higher compared to those seen for the sdAb42 lines (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve and fluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: While sdAb BCII10 levels remain stable over time, sdAb42 levels decrease rapidly.
source: In addition, we observed that, while sdAb BCII10 levels remain stable over time, sdAb42 levels decrease rapidly (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in sdAb42 levels is the result of a parasite defense mechanism at the translational but not transcriptional level.
source: We suspect that this is the result of a parasite defense mechanism at the translational but not transcriptional level (sdAb42 transcript levels remain stable, data not shown) to specifically counter sdAb42 (but not BCII10) production.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that sdAb42 protein levels decrease while transcript levels remain stable.

claim: Antibodies are valuable drug discovery tools.
source: Indeed, antibodies (or fragments thereof) are valuable drug discovery tools.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of drug discovery.

claim: Antibodies and camelid sdAbs are known for their ability to 'freeze out' specific conformations of highly dynamic antigens.
source: Antibodies (and camelid sdAbs especially) are known for their ability to 'freeze out' specific conformations of highly dynamic antigens, thereby exposing target sites of interest, which could be exploited for rational drug design (Lawson, 2012; Khamrui et al., 2013; van Dongen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lawson, 2012; Khamrui et al., 2013; and van Dongen et al., 2019.

claim: Achieving trypanosome death through TbrPYK inhibition would require an 88% reduction in the enzyme's Vmax.
source: Earlier work by Albert and colleagues suggests that achieving trypanosome death through TbrPYK inhibition would require an 88% reduction in the enzyme's Vmax, thereby resulting in lowering the glycolytic flux below 50% (Albert et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Albert et al., 2005.

claim: Trypanosomes cannot survive more than 12 hr in a situation wherein their ATP synthesis flux is reduced by harvesting only 1 instead of 2 ATP molecules per glucose molecule.
source: This is consistent with the observation that trypanosomes cannot survive more than 12 hr in a situation wherein their ATP synthesis flux is reduced by harvesting only 1 instead of 2 ATP molecules per glucose molecule (Helfert et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Helfert et al., 2001.

claim: Novel trypanosomatid PYK inhibitors should be used in concert with inhibitors of trypanosomatid glucose transporters and PFK to achieve synergistic effects.
source: Hence, it has been proposed that novel trypanosomatid PYK inhibitors should be used in concert with inhibitors of trypanosomatid glucose transporters and PFK to achieve synergistic effects (Haanstra et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haanstra et al., 2011.

claim: Trypanosomes are known to mainly regulate gene expression through extensive post-transcriptional mechanisms.
source: While the exact mechanism remains unknown, trypanosomes are known to mainly regulate gene expression through extensive post-transcriptional mechanisms (Clayton, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clayton, 2019.

claim: sdAb42 may pinpoint a site of vulnerability on trypanosomatid PYKs that could potentially be exploited for the design of novel chemotherapeutics.
source: Based on the presented results, we propose that sdAb42 may pinpoint a site of vulnerability on trypanosomatid PYKs that could potentially be exploited for the design of novel chemotherapeutics.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: TcoPYK was previously identified as a biomarker for the detection of active T. congolense infections.
source: sdAb42 was originally identified within a diagnostic context, in which its target TcoPYK was shown to be a reliable biomarker for the detection of active T. congolense infections (Pinto Torres et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pinto Torres et al., 2018.

claim: The location of the sdAb42-recognized 'allosteric hotspot' is reminiscent of the binding site for free amino acids found in human PYKs.
source: Interestingly, the location of this 'allosteric hotspot' is reminiscent of the binding site for free amino acids found in human PYKs (Chaneton et al., 2012; Yuan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison, supported by citations to Chaneton et al., 2012 and Yuan et al., 2018.

claim: Various amino acids have been shown to be allosteric regulators of human PYK activity.
source: Indeed, various amino acids have been shown to be allosteric regulators of human PYK activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about human PYK regulation.

claim: PYKs from different species have evolved different allosteric strategies to regulate enzyme activity.
source: This resonates with the previous finding that PYKs from different species have evolved different allosteric strategies to regulate enzyme activity and that these differences could be exploited in drug discovery (Morgan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morgan et al., 2014.

claim: The epitope is significantly distorted when TcoPYK transitions from the T to the R state (Cα RMSD of 3.70 Å).
source: A first finding that supports this idea is that the sdAb42 epitope is significantly distorted when TcoPYK transitions from the T to the R state (Cα RMSD of 3.70 Å, Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sulfate molecules were found in the TcoPYK effector site at the positions usually occupied by the phosphoryl groups of fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
source: A detailed inspection of the electron density revealed the presence of sulfate molecules in the TcoPYK effector site at the positions usually occupied by the phosphoryl groups of the cognate effector molecules fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Despite the presence of sulfates, TcoPYK clearly remains in a T state conformation when bound by sdAb42.
source: Despite the presence of these sulfates, TcoPYK clearly remains in a T state conformation when bound by sdAb42.
evidence: This claim is supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The in silico ΔΔG analysis predicts that the single Ile352Val and triple Lys43Gln/Val348Ala/Ile352Leu mutations are expected to have a negative impact on binding energy.
source: The impact of these differences on binding energy was first assessed through an in silico ΔΔ G analysis, which predicts that the single Ile352Val (corresponding TbrPYK epitope) and triple Lys43Gln/Val348Ala/Ile352Leu (corresponding LmePYK epitope) mutations are expected to have a negative impact on binding energy and thus affinity (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis data shown in Table 2.

claim: The 400-fold difference between the KD and IC50 values has been observed for the sdAb-mediated allosteric inhibition of other kinases.
source: Although we currently do not have a mechanistic explanation, similar differences have been observed for the sdAb-mediated allosteric inhibition of other kinases (Singh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2022.

claim: Genetic engineering and culturing of T. congolense is notoriously difficult.
source: Since genetic engineering and culturing of T. congolense is notoriously difficult (Awuah-Mensah et al., 2021), we opted to perform our experiments in T. brucei.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Awuah-Mensah et al., 2021.

claim: A rapid loss of sdAb42 intrabody was noted, resulting in heterogenous in situ expression levels.
source: A rapid loss of sdAb42 intrabody was noted, resulting in heterogenous in situ expression levels.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The chemotherapeutic targeting of enzymes involved in energy metabolism has long shown promise in the battle against parasitic protists.
source: The chemotherapeutic targeting of enzymes involved in energy metabolism has long shown promise in the battle against parasitic protists.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of antiparasitic drug development.

claim: Many parasitic protists heavily rely on glycolysis within their vertebrate hosts to sustain their energy metabolism.
source: First, many parasitic protists heavily rely on glycolysis within their vertebrate hosts to sustain their energy metabolism: Giardia spp. trophozoites, Trichomonas spp., Entamoeba spp. trophozoites, Plasmodium spp. intraerythrocytic stages, Leishmania spp., Trypanosoma spp. BSFs (Eisenthal and Cornish-Bowden, 1998; Upcroft and Upcroft, 2001; Saunders et al., 2010; Alam et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Eisenthal and Cornish-Bowden, 1998; Upcroft and Upcroft, 2001; Saunders et al., 2010; Alam et al., 2014).

claim: The glycolytic enzymes and transporters of parasitic protists are sufficiently different from their vertebrate host homologs such that they may be specifically targeted.
source: Second, the glycolytic enzymes and transporters are sufficiently different from their vertebrate host homologs such that they may be specifically targeted.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the potential for selective targeting of parasite enzymes.

claim: Recent work on T. brucei and Cryptosporidium parvum demonstrates that achieving parasite killing by inhibiting glycolysis remains a viable avenue.
source: Recent work on T. brucei and Cryptosporidium parvum demonstrates that achieving parasite killing by inhibiting glycolysis remains a viable avenue (McNae et al., 2021; Khan et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McNae et al., 2021 and Khan et al., 2023.
